headline: South Windsor votes to end Flock contract and remove license-plate readers
dek: The Town Council voted 6-3 to take down eight automated license-plate readers within 60 days and purge the data, putting privacy concerns ahead of keeping the system as a police tool.
body: South Windsor will end its contract with Flock Safety and remove the town’s automated license-plate readers after the Town Council voted 6-3 Monday night. The resolution calls for the town manager to terminate the agreement, take down the readers within 60 days and purge the data collected through the system, according to the [Journal Inquirer’s report](https://www.ctinsider.com/journalinquirer/article/south-windsor-ct-flock-cameras-removed-22465434.php).

The decision followed an Oct. 5 public hearing on the eight cameras. The Journal Inquirer reported that residents from South Windsor and neighboring communities spoke in favor of removal, with privacy and Fourth Amendment concerns dominating the testimony. No one at the hearing spoke in favor of keeping the system, the newspaper reported. A council straw poll after the hearing produced a 20-2 vote for removal, although the formal council action was the 6-3 vote that sets the town’s policy.

Mayor Craig Zimmerman said he initially supported the program but changed his position after meeting with officials inside and outside South Windsor. He told the Journal Inquirer that the cameras could help police, but that he was not comfortable with the contract’s limits on control and accountability for the data. Deputy Mayor Andrew Paterna similarly framed the vote as a question about mass surveillance rather than distrust of South Windsor police.

The three council members who opposed removal emphasized the public-safety value of the technology. Councilor Audrey Delnicki described Flock and similar systems as another tool available to law enforcement, while Councilor Michael Ouellette said he trusted the police chief and department to handle the data appropriately, according to the Journal Inquirer. Councilor Elizabeth Pendleton said she was initially undecided before voting to remove the cameras because a private company operated the system and had access to extensive personal data.

South Windsor’s own April 6 council minutes show how the system was designed to work before Monday’s vote. Police Chief Kristian Lindstrom described four bidirectional locations that scanned roadways in both directions and said the system had been operating for nearly 11 months. The minutes say ordinary data was stored for 30 days unless it was retained longer for an investigation, and that officers used individual accounts with trackable credentials. Those details came from a presentation months before the council chose to end the program, not from an audit of the vote or a finding that South Windsor officers misused the system. The [town minutes](https://www.southwindsor-ct.gov/sites/g/files/vyhlif8416/f/minutes/4-6-26_minutes-town-council-regular-meeting_2.pdf) provide that earlier official account.

The local decision arrives as Connecticut’s new automated-license-plate-reader rules take effect. The Connecticut Office of Legislative Research says Public Act 26-14, effective Oct. 1, generally limits retention to 21 days and restricts public agencies and vendors to listed uses, including specific criminal investigations, warrant searches, missing-person cases and stolen-vehicle recovery. The law also bars certain forms of monitoring and data use, including investigations tied to immigration enforcement. The [legislative summary](https://www.cga.ct.gov/2026/rpt/pdf/2026-R-0089.pdf) describes the statewide framework, but it does not require South Windsor to keep its local system operating.

Flock spokeswoman Courtney Terlecki told the Journal Inquirer that agencies own their data, access is limited to authorized users and searches create permanent audit trails. South Windsor’s vote does not decide whether other Connecticut towns will keep similar systems, but it adds another local test of whether the investigative benefits are worth the privacy and governance concerns. The Journal Inquirer has reported that the town began using the readers in 2025 after the council approved the program in a 2023 executive session.

For residents, the immediate change is operational: the readers are scheduled to come down, the contract is to be terminated and the collected data is to be purged. If South Windsor officials later propose bringing the technology back, the Journal Inquirer reported that the town would need another public hearing and another public vote. That leaves the next steps—contract timing, physical removal and confirmation of deletion—as the parts of Monday’s decision that still have to be carried out.
location: South Windsor Town Hall, South Windsor, Connecticut
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: South Windsor votes to remove Flock license-plate readers
